## What you’ll do

You’ll have **2 hours on a group call** to build a small product using Node.js or TypeScript, React, MongoDB, and Redis. You get **10 minutes to read and start services, 100 minutes to build, and 10 minutes to run the final check and submit**. Join five minutes early.

The brief deliberately asks for more than fits in the time. They’re grading what you prioritize, how you verify it, and whether your app behaves correctly through network problems, process restarts, and multiple instances running at once. You can run their checker as often as you like.

## The rules

- **Work alone.** AI tools are allowed and expected. Documentation, search, your own notes and snippets, and any Node framework or libraries are allowed. Ask assessment questions in the shared channel so everyone sees the answers.
- **Export every AI conversation you use** into the repository’s `ai-logs/` folder.
- **Commit at least every 15 minutes.**
- **Create a new GitHub repository on assessment day.** Keep it private while you build, make it public when you submit, and leave it public and unchanged for **14 days**.
- **Push your final commit and send the form before the two-hour cutoff.** They take a snapshot at the cutoff, so later pushes won’t count.

## What you submit

- **GitHub repo** with your code and commit history, a README that lets someone run it from a clean clone, a half-page note explaining your decisions, your last checker report, and your AI transcripts.
- **Submission form** with your name, email, repo URL, final commit ID, and the AI tools you used.

## What to prepare

At least a day before, check that **Node 22, Git, and Docker Desktop** work, that Docker has about **4 GB of memory free**, and that you can push to GitHub from your terminal. Pre-pull `mongo:7`, `redis:7-alpine`, and `node:22-alpine`. Elasticsearch `8.15.3` is optional. Run `node doctor.js --preflight` and address any `WARN` results. Make sure your AI tool can export conversations.

If you’re shortlisted, there’s a **30-minute follow-up** where you’ll explain your decisions and debug a failure in your own submission, including any code AI helped write.

can you now tell me what is the project of about what you did in that project what is the architecture etc basically what you build?

**Switchboard is a shared customer-support inbox.** Think of Acme and Globex as two companies using the same app. Each company’s agents sign in, see their own customer conversations arrive live, claim a conversation, reply, close or reopen it, and leave encrypted private notes for coworkers.

**How it’s built**

- **React + Vite** provides the inbox and conversation view. It uses HTTP for actions and WebSockets for live updates. When the browser reconnects, it asks for events after the last sequence number it received.
- **Express + TypeScript** handles login, workspace access, the inbox API, and webhooks from Pigeon, the simulated messaging provider. Login uses OpenID Connect with PKCE. The server checks workspace membership on both the API and WebSockets.
- **MongoDB** stores conversations, messages, pending replies, and live event history. A version check makes concurrent updates safe. That’s what lets exactly one agent win when several try to claim the same conversation.
- **Redis** stores short-lived login state and sessions so any server instance can recognize a signed-in agent.

**What happens when a customer messages you:** Pigeon sends a signed webhook. The server verifies it, checks for duplicates, and saves the message before acknowledging it. The inbox then updates over WebSocket. When an agent replies, the server saves the reply first and a worker sends it to Pigeon. If a worker crashes or the provider times out, the retry reuses the same idempotency key so the customer doesn’t get the reply twice.

Private notes are encrypted in the browser with a shared workspace key. The server stores ciphertext. I deferred optional search and billing to focus on the inbox and failure recovery. The main scaling tradeoff is that each workspace’s data currently lives in one MongoDB document, which simplifies atomic updates but limits how much history a workspace can retain.

The public checker passed **75/75**, and the larger three-instance test passed **37/37**.

**Sign-in is required. Sign-up is outside the project scope.** The brief asks us to integrate the supplied **mock identity provider** using OpenID Connect with PKCE. The screen where you click a name is the provider’s built-in test login. It deliberately has no passwords or registration. Our app still verifies the signed identity token, checks the login state and nonce, sets an HttpOnly session cookie, and checks workspace membership on both the API and WebSocket. In production, the real identity provider would handle passwords, MFA, or whatever sign-in policy the company uses.

**The names and numbers came from the starter or its simulators.**

- **Asha Rao, Ben Ortiz, Chloe Martin, Dev Patel, and Eli Novak** are listed in `START_HERE.md`. Acme and Globex are the supplied workspaces.
- The customer **phone numbers** are listed in `PIGEON.md` and used by the simulator. Incoming sample texts come from Pigeon. The reply and private note you may see locally were typed by me during the browser smoke test.
- **75/75** and **37/37** are results I measured. The first is from the supplied full checker. The second is from an extra run with three server instances and more replies. The assessor-only level was unavailable locally.

**The main choices I made where the brief left room:**

- I put each workspace’s state, reply queue, and event history in one MongoDB document so a single atomic write can update both the data and its live event. That trades storage headroom and write efficiency for a simpler, reliable first version.
- I used Redis for login state and sessions, and made WebSockets read their replay history from MongoDB. The brief required reconnect and multi-instance replay. It left the mechanism open.
- I chose a 30-conversation page size and used message ID as a tie-breaker when two messages have the same timestamp. I allowed replies on closed threads because the brief didn’t specify a sending restriction.
- For encrypted notes, I chose a workspace key that members share through a trusted channel. Search and billing were optional and I left them out.

The [brief](C:/Users/vansh/Downloads/preflight/starter/BRIEF.md) describes the requirements. The [decisions note](C:/Users/vansh/Downloads/preflight/starter/DECISIONS.md) records the implementation choices and tradeoffs.
